texts.full_text: challenge. The thing we can do something about is the quality of our transport network. It is sobering to look at the scale of investment in the motorway networks comparing the UK with the two dominating economies in the EU, France and Germany. The number of motorway miles constructed in France and Germany since 2000 is 850 and 680 miles respectively. The figure for the UK is 46 miles. France has a motorway network of 7000 miles, Germany 8000 miles and the UK 2300. Admittedly France and Germany are bigger, but not that much bigger, and the density indicator for traffic on UK motorways is 113 with the equivalent figures in Germany and France of 39 and 47. These are big and significant disparities. It is not hard to see why we have congested roads. Next, some figures on the quality of the road network which were produced by the Institute of Civil Engineers in their 2014 State of the Nation report. The strategic network for the UK received a B grade, which means “adequate for now”, and the local network received a D - grade, which means at risk. There is a significant disparity between the strategic network and local road networks and this imbalance is another particular feature of the UK. If you want to go on a journey from A to B, you do not think I will be ok most of the way, you want to get from A to B. Over the next 5 years Highways England funding is set to double, which is fine, but in comparison local government funding has been cut year on year since 2010 and in spite of a modest increase in local highways maintenance in 2015, the future looks bleak. To compound this, the local road network is in a far worst state of repair than the strategic network and this leads to higher vehicle operating costs.

texts.full_text: Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma in a reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus). An 8-year-old female adult reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus) was referred to the Veterinary Hospital of Madrid for evaluation of a conjunctival mass on the left eye which had been present for about 2 months. A surgical excision was performed and biopsy material submitted for light microscopic evaluation which confirmed the diagnosis of conjuctival squamous cell carcinoma. Nuclear p53 immunolabeling was found in 52% of the neoplastic cells. Follow-up examination at 12months post-surgery revealed no evidence of recurrence or metastasis. Conjunctival Squamous Cell Carcinomas (SCCs) are relatively rare but aggressive malignancies that typically affect older individuals, particularly those with a history of sun exposure and conjuctivitis. In reindeer specifically, such cases have been reported to be even more uncommon due in part their habitat which is often less exposed directly sunlight. In the case described here involving an 8-year-old female adult Rangifer tarandus.tarandus (cervine), it was noted that she had a conjunctival mass on her left eye, present for about two months. The reindeer were referred to Veterinary Hospital of Madrid where they performed surgical excision and biopsy material submitted under light microscopic evaluation confirmed the diagnosis as squamous cell carcinoma. Nuclear p53 immunolabeling was found in 52% of neoplastic cells which indicates that there is a potential for genetic mutation or instability within these cancerous tissues. P53, also known as tumor suppressor protein (TSP), plays an important role by preventing the formation and growths of tumors. Post-surgery follow-up examination conducted at twelve months postoperative showed no evidence recurrence nor metastasis which suggests that surgical intervention was effective in managing this case. In conclusion: The occurrence conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma is extremely rare among reindeer, but it does happen. Early detection and prompt treatment are crucial for a successful outcome as illustrated by the reported success of surgery on our patient. texts.full_text: n period in PDT by ionizing ALA using direct-current pulsed iontophoresis to treat actinic keratosis (AK). Twenty percent ALA solution was applied to AK lesions of five patients using a custom-made device that delivers 0.5 mA/cm² for 20 minutes at the treatment site, immediately followed by PDT using red light with a wavelength of approximately 630 nm and an energy density of 75 J/cm². The results showed significant improvement in ALA absorption within as little as 15-30 minutes after iontophoresis compared to traditional passive diffusion methods. All patients experienced complete resolution or marked reduction in lesion size at the follow-up evaluation conducted one month post-treatment, with minimal side effects reported such as mild erythema and transient stinging sensation during treatment. In conclusion, direct-current pulsed iontophoresis can effectively enhance ALA absorption for PDT of AK lesions, potentially reducing the required pre-illumination waiting time. This technique may offer a more efficient alternative to conventional application methods in clinical settings where rapid onset is desired or patient compliance with prolonged incubation periods poses challenges.
